title: Good Taste Is a Bias
author: Tom Stafford
summary: Cognitive scientist Tom Stafford examines a structural dilemma in any system that relies on multiple human judges scoring different sets of things -- teachers marking essays, football scouts rating players, or grant reviewers scoring funding proposals -- namely that a judge's tendency to be generous or ungenerous (their 'bias' in the statistical sense) is mathematically indistinguishable from that judge simply having been handed a genuinely weaker or stronger batch of things to judge. He walks through the statistical fix, 'normalisation,' which adjusts every judge's scores to share the same mean and variance so they land on a common scale, then shows its cost with a worked example: a judge's honest 28-out-of-100 for a genuinely poor essay gets silently reinterpreted by the math as evidence the judge is simply ungenerous. Drawing on his own consulting work with research funders, Stafford reports that most funding bodies do not normalise reviewer scores despite this being the textbook-correct approach, and offers a two-part explanation: normalisation sacrifices the simple legibility of 'judges give a score, that's it' for a statistically sound but harder-to-explain and harder-to-trust process, and it also risks flattening a genuinely discerning judge (who sees real quality variation) together with a merely generous one (who gives everything a 10 regardless of merit) into the same corrected profile. His conclusion is that normalisation trades away exactly the individual discernment -- 'discrimination' in its original sense of perceiving real differences -- that makes a good judge valuable in the first place.
points: The core mathematical dilemma is that a judge's honest 28-out-of-100 score for a genuinely weak object is statistically indistinguishable from that judge simply being 'ungenerous' -- normalisation cannot tell the two apart, and by construction treats them identically.

Stafford's finding from consulting with research funders -- that most do not normalise reviewer scores despite the statistically correct approach recommending it -- is offered as a real-world data point that complicates the assumption that standardisation is always the responsible choice.

The legibility argument reframes 'not normalising' as a deliberate trade: judges giving a raw, unadjusted score is easy to explain and trust, while a corrected score (a raw 28 becoming -1.12) opens a new front of doubt about the judging process itself, undermining its legitimacy even as it improves its statistical accuracy.

The essay's sharpest point is that normalisation cannot distinguish a truly discerning judge (who gives genuinely differentiated scores because they perceive real quality variation) from a merely careless or overly generous one (who gives uniform high scores) -- both get flattened by the same statistical correction, destroying exactly the discriminating signal a good judge provides.
quotes: Here is the root of the dilemma — how should you weight opinions from different judges? Taking all judgements at face value risks the outcome being skewed by an outlier or miscalibrated judge. Aggregating the scores from different judges to correct for miscalibration risks throwing away the unique and valuable signal that each judge provides.

The adjustment has taken away something. What if Judge A really did mean to award 28 out of 100? Object 3 is a stinker. The normalisation process is, in effect, declaring that Judge A is ungenerous, because they gave low scores, but maybe they just got dealt low quality objects to judge?
For what it is worth, some funders normalise the scores they get from different reviews. Most don't.
Judging has two functions: to deliver a score, and to legitimate that score. The ingredients for this legitimacy are a curious blend of transparency and inscrutability.
Not-normalising may be statistically sub-optimal, but it is easy to explain. Judges give a score. That's it.

A judge who gave away all 10s because they are overly generous looks exactly like a judge who gave all 10s because they really did mean to award 10s to what they saw, and what they saw really was worth it.
